title: Plural of older -i word families
summary: For these older -i families, keep dictionary-form i and add -a/-ä: ovi (“door”) → ovia.
objectives: Form the plural partitive in this bounded word family.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: A case is a word form used for a grammatical job. The dictionary form is the form used to look up a word. The partitive has several uses; it does not always mean “some”. Here you practise forming the word, so no sentence construction is required.

The selected older -i words keep their dictionary-form i and add -a/-ä in the plural partitive. Their singular partitives can use e or a changing consonant stem, but those singular changes are not copied into these plural forms. This shared plural rule covers the selected ovi, vesi and pieni families. Short newer -i words instead have the separately taught -eja/-ejä pattern.
keyPoints: Learn each word with its pattern; a similar final letter does not guarantee the same stem.

steps: Keep final i and add -a: ovi → ovia.
The word’s meaning stays connected to “door”; its plural case form changes its grammatical use.
Keep final i and add -ä: järvi → järviä.
The word’s meaning stays connected to “lake”; its plural case form changes its grammatical use.
Keep final i and add -ä: nimi → nimiä.
The word’s meaning stays connected to “name”; its plural case form changes its grammatical use.
Keep dictionary-form si and add -ä: vesi → vesiä.
The word’s meaning stays connected to “water”; its plural case form changes its grammatical use.
Keep dictionary-form si and add -ä: käsi → käsiä.
The word’s meaning stays connected to “hand”; its plural case form changes its grammatical use.
Keep final i and add -ä: pieni → pieniä.
The word’s meaning stays connected to “small”; its plural case form changes its grammatical use.
Keep dictionary-form psi and add -a: lapsi → lapsia.
The word’s meaning stays connected to “child”; its plural case form changes its grammatical use.
Keep final i and add -ä: kieli → kieliä.
The word’s meaning stays connected to “language”; its plural case form changes its grammatical use.

commonMistakes: Keep dictionary-form i in these plurals.
Do not reuse the singular e or consonant stem.
Do not apply this bounded rule to newer -i words.
